shown.title: The old oak
shown.hook: Two hundred years old, and leaning over the school path.
shown.setup: The oak on the village green is about two hundred years old. It leans over the path to the school, and in March a big branch came down in the night. There is fungus at its base. The parish has left the decision to you, and the autumn storms are five weeks away.
shown.uncertain: Whether a hollowing, leaning oak will stand through the storms.

steps.prompt: Before you decide, you can find things out. Each takes time, and the work itself will need the last week.

facts.label: Ask the tree surgeon to climb it
facts.text: The crown is full of leaf. She says cutting it back would ease the strain, and that big cuts on an old oak can let rot in.

facts.label: Find old photographs of the green
facts.text: In a photograph from 1952 the oak leans exactly as far as it does today. There is no fungus in the photograph.

facts.label: Have the trunk scanned
facts.text: About a third of the trunk is hollow. Hollow oaks often stand for decades; some don’t.

bands.risks: acting on a lean and some fungus alone
facts that still don’t settle it

options.text: Fell it
options.detail: No more risk from it, and no more oak.
options.risks: felling a tree that would have stood for decades

options.text: Take a third of the weight off the crown
options.detail: It stays, smaller. Less likely to fall; the cuts are for good.
options.costs: a third of the crown, for good
options.risks: rot in the cuts, or a fall anyway

options.text: Leave it, and fence off the path
options.detail: The oak stays as it is. The children walk round by the road.
options.costs: a longer walk to school while it stands
options.risks: the oak coming down inside the fence

cases.fell: The oak comes down in a day. The stump is wider than a kitchen table, and a boy from the school counts 214 rings. The path is open again by Friday.
cases.crown: The tree surgeon spends two days in the crown. From the pub the oak looks thinner, and still very much itself. The path stays open, and the storms will test it.
cases.fence: A fence goes up around the oak, and the school sends a letter about the longer walk. The oak meets the storms as it is.

ending.others: Some fell it at once. Some spend three weeks on the scan, because a felled oak can’t be put back. Some fence it off and let the children walk round.

facts.fact: A hollowing trunk is a natural process in old trees, and not necessarily a sign of an ailing one.

real.invented: The oak, the green, what each check finds and the five weeks are invented.

shown.title: The harvest
shown.hook: Every day the grapes get sweeter. A storm may be coming.
shown.setup: Your grapes are nearly ripe. Each extra day on the vine makes them sweeter and the wine better. A storm may be on its way: if it hits before you pick, the rain will split half the grapes. Picking takes your crew one full day, and the forecast changes every morning.
shown.uncertain: Whether the storm comes, and when.

days.label: Monday
days.text: Forecast: a three-in-ten chance of a storm this week, most likely Friday. This far ahead, forecasts are often a day or two out. Picked today, a good, light wine.

days.label: Tuesday
days.text: Forecast: five in ten, Thursday or Friday. Picked today, a good wine.

days.label: Wednesday
days.text: Forecast: seven in ten, on Friday, perhaps Thursday night. Picked today, a very good wine.

days.label: Thursday
days.text: Forecast: nine in ten, from Friday midday. Storms like this sometimes arrive a day early. Picked today, the best wine in years.

steps.last: Wait for the storm to pass

bands.costs: four days of watching the sky
bands.risks: rain on the last rows if the storm comes early

cases.mon: Your crew picks on Monday in sunshine. Every grape is in, whatever the week brings: a good, light wine.
cases.tue: You pick on Tuesday, before the forecasts firm up. Every grape is in: a good wine, whatever the storm does.
cases.wed: You pick on Wednesday under a high, thin sky. Every grape is in: a very good wine, whatever Friday brings.
cases.thu: You pick all Thursday under a darkening sky. If the storm keeps to its forecast, every grape is in: the best wine in years. If it comes a day early, rain catches the last rows.
cases.out: You wait. If the storm misses, as it does one time in ten, you’ll make an extraordinary wine. If it comes, you lose half the crop, and the half that’s left is still very fine.

ending.others: Some pick on Monday: a good wine in hand beats a better one in the forecast. Some wait for Wednesday’s clearer news. A few hold on for Thursday’s sugar, or let the storm decide.

facts.fact: Heavy rain close to harvest can split a large share of ripe grapes.

sources.name: University of Wisconsin Fruit Program, “Berry splitting in grapes, should you harvest?” (2020)

real.invented: The vineyard, the forecasts and “half the grapes” are invented.

shown.title: Your uncle’s boat
shown.hook: A wooden boat, a fair offer, and a summer you haven’t had yet.
shown.setup: Your uncle has left you his wooden sailing boat. You’ve never sailed. A buyer has made a fair offer, good until Friday. Keeping her means a mooring fee every month and weekends of sanding and varnish. Sailing lessons start at the harbour next week: by autumn, you’d know whether you like it.

options.text: Sell her on Friday
options.detail: A fair price now. You’d learn in the club’s dinghies.
options.risks: loving sailing, in someone else’s boat

options.text: Keep her for the summer, then decide
options.detail: Mooring and upkeep until autumn. The buyer may not wait.
options.costs: a summer of fees and sanding
options.risks: losing the buyer

options.text: Keep her, whatever happens
options.detail: She stays in the family, and so do the fees.
options.costs: fees for as long as you keep her
options.risks: a boat that never leaves her mooring

ask.label: Ask at the sailing club first
ask.answer: The club would take her for the season and teach beginners on her. No fees for you. She’d be theirs until October, so no sale before then, and beginners are hard on boats.

adds.text: Lend her to the club for the season
adds.detail: No fees, no sale until October, and beginners at the helm.
adds.costs: a season of wear on her

cases.sell: The buyer sails her away on Saturday and promises a photo from the water. Your lessons start in a club dinghy. If you love it, there will be other boats, though not this one.
cases.summer: You pay the mooring and spend Saturdays sanding. By autumn you’ll know about sailing. Whether the buyer will still be interested, the story doesn’t say.
cases.always: You paint her name fresh on the stern. Whether you’ll sail her, the summer will tell. She’s yours either way.
cases.club: The club takes her for the season, and beginners learn on her, you among them. By October you’ll know about sailing, and she’ll have the scrapes to show for it.

ending.others: Some sell on Friday: a fair price is certain, and there are other boats to learn in. Some pay to keep the question open until the lessons answer it. Some keep her whatever happens.

shown.title: The new loaf
shown.hook: Eleven years of the same six breads. Now, maybe, a seventh.
shown.setup: Your bakery has sold the same six breads for eleven years, and your regulars like it that way. One night you worked out a seventh: dark rye with figs and fennel. You love it. You have no idea whether anyone else will.
shown.uncertain: Whether anyone but you will want the new bread.
shown.turnsOn: putting the new bread on sale

steps.prompt: What do you do with it first?

options.text: Put twelve on the shelf on Saturday
options.detail: Costs a batch. If they don’t sell, you stop.
options.risks: loaves coming home unsold

options.text: Hand out tasting slices all week
options.detail: Costs a week and half a batch. You hear what people say.
options.costs: a week and half a batch
options.risks: kind words that never become sales

options.text: Give a loaf each to three regulars
options.detail: Costs three loaves. You hear from people who know your bread.
options.risks: three opinions standing in for everyone

cases.shelf: By closing time on Saturday, seven of the twelve have gone. A man in a green coat asks whether it will be there next week. Five come home with you.
cases.taste: All week the slices disappear. Most people say it’s lovely, a few say “interesting”, and one asks what fennel is. Nobody asks to buy a loaf.
cases.regulars: Two of them love it. Mrs Okafor says the fennel is far too strong, and that she’d buy it anyway.

options.text: Bake it every Saturday
options.risks: Saturdays of loaves coming home

options.text: Change the recipe, then try again
options.risks: losing what the first version had

options.text: Keep it as your own bread, not the shop’s
options.risks: never finding out

cases.weekly: It goes up on the board as the seventh bread. Over the winter you’ll find out what eleven years of regulars make of it.
cases.change: You take out half the fennel and try again in a fortnight. The rye stays dark.
cases.own: You bake it on Sundays, for the house. The six breads carry on as they were.

ending.others: Some put it straight on the shelf: a batch is cheap to lose, and only a sale shows who would buy it. Some ask first, because a shelf can’t tell you why a loaf didn’t sell.

shown.title: The last of the light
shown.hook: The best take of the day, and no way to see it until Thursday.
shown.setup: You’re directing a small film, shot on 16mm film. On the last evening at the lighthouse, take four of the farewell scene felt right: she held the pause before her last line. There’s light for one more set-up. Film can’t be seen until a lab develops it, and this evening’s reels come back on Thursday, after the crew has left the island.
shown.uncertain: Whether take four is as good on film as it felt on set.
shown.turnsOn: spending the last light on the wide shot

steps.prompt: What do you use the last light for?

options.text: Another take of the scene
options.detail: A second chance if take four has a fault. The film ends without its wide shot.
options.risks: a second take with faults of its own

options.text: The wide shot of the lighthouse
options.detail: The ending you planned. Take four is your only good take.
options.risks: a fault in take four, with no other take

ask.label: Ask the camera operator about take four
ask.answer: She watched it through the lens. “The frame was right, and it looked sharp to me. On film, you only know on Thursday.”

cases.again: You shoot take five as the light goes, and she rushes the pause a little. The reels leave on the morning boat. On Thursday the lab will show which take holds her last line. The film will end on her face, not the lighthouse.
cases.wide: The wide shot catches the last light on the lighthouse, and the crew packs up in the dark. The reels leave on the morning boat. On Thursday the lab will show whether take four is as good on film as it felt.

ending.others: Some shoot the scene again: the film can’t be checked, so a second take is the only cover. Some take the wide shot: take four felt right, and the ending matters too.

facts.fact: Film has to be developed before anyone can see what it caught. In the film era, each day’s footage went to a lab overnight and was watched later as “dailies”.

sources.name: Roland Denning, “The golden age of film laboratories”, RedShark News (2023)

facts.fact: On a film camera only the operator looks through the lens; the focus puller works from marks and judgement, and a soft shot can’t be made sharp afterwards.

real.invented: The film, the island, the takes and the lab’s Thursday are invented. Digital footage can be checked at once; this story is shot on film.

shown.title: The last packet
shown.hook: Ten rows, and a packet of beans nobody grows any more.
shown.setup: At the village seed swap, an old man presses a packet of climbing beans into your hand: a local kind nobody sells any more. Seeds this old don’t keep. Each year fewer will sprout, and in a few years none will. Your plot has ten rows, and your household eats from it all summer.
shown.uncertain: How many of the old seeds are still alive.

steps.prompt: How do you plant your ten rows this spring?

items.detail: Nobody knows how many will come up.

bands.risks: too few plants to save seed

cases.none: You keep the packet in a drawer, and the plot gives you its usual summer. Next spring, fewer of the beans will sprout; the spring after, fewer still.
cases.few: About one seed in three comes up. By September a handful of plants hang heavy with pods: just enough fresh seed to try again next year. The rest of the plot does what it always does.
cases.many: About one seed in three comes up, so those rows stand half empty and you buy vegetables in August. By September there is fresh seed to give away at next year’s swap.
cases.all: About one seed in three comes up, so the whole plot stands half empty and you buy vegetables all summer. By September there is more fresh seed than next year’s swap can take.

ending.others: Some plant none: the household eats from those rows. Some give it a row or two, enough to save fresh seed. Some give it half the plot, because a kind that’s lost is lost for good.

facts.fact: Bean seed keeps for two to four years on average, longest when it is stored cool and dry.

sources.name: Johnny’s Selected Seeds, “Seed viability and seed storage guidelines”

real.invented: The packet, its age and “one seed in three” are invented.

shown.whatIf: What if the forecasts stopped after Monday?
shown.title: The harvest, without forecasts
shown.hook: The same grapes, the same storm, and no more news.
shown.setup: Your grapes are nearly ripe, and each extra day on the vine makes the wine better. Monday’s forecast gives a three-in-ten chance of a storm this week, most likely Friday: if it hits before you pick, the rain will split half the grapes. Then the forecasts stop. The station is down until next week. Picking everything takes your crew one full day.
shown.uncertain: Whether the storm comes, and when, with no more news.

steps.prompt: With no more forecasts, how do you pick?

options.text: Pick everything today
options.detail: A good, light wine, whatever the week brings.
options.risks: nothing from the storm

options.text: Pick half today, the rest on Thursday
options.detail: Half a light wine now, half a rich one if the storm keeps to Friday.
options.risks: the second half, if the storm comes early

options.text: Wait, and pick the day the barometer falls
options.detail: It has fallen before most storms here. Not every one.
options.risks: a storm that comes without warning

cases.now: Your crew picks on Monday in sunshine. Every grape is in, whatever the week brings: a good, light wine.
cases.half: Half the grapes come in on Monday, light and clean. The rest hang until Thursday: if the storm keeps to Friday, a rich wine to blend with the light one. If it comes early, rain splits the second half.
cases.glass: You tap the barometer every morning. If it falls first, your crew picks at once: the longer it held, the sweeter the wine. If the storm comes without warning, it splits half the crop.

ending.others: Some pick at once: with no news coming, waiting is a bet. Some split the crop between two days. Some decide now what will make them pick, and watch for it.

facts.fact: Heavy rain close to harvest can split a large share of ripe grapes.

sources.name: University of Wisconsin Fruit Program, “Berry splitting in grapes, should you harvest?” (2020)

real.invented: The vineyard, the forecasts, the broken station, the barometer’s record and “half the grapes” are invented.

shown.whatIf: What if she would sell just as well next spring?

options.text: Keep her for the summer, then decide

options.costs: a summer of fees and sanding
options.risks: a summer that doesn’t settle it

options.text: Keep her, whatever happens
options.detail: She stays in the family, and so do the fees.
options.costs: fees for as long as you keep her
options.risks: a boat that never leaves her mooring

adds.detail: No fees, no sale until October, and beginners at the helm.

cases.summer: You pay the mooring and spend Saturdays sanding. By autumn you’ll know about sailing. If it isn’t for you, she goes to the broker in spring.

shown.whatIf: What if a second camera had filmed the scene from the side?
shown.title: The last of the light, with a second camera
shown.hook: The same take, and a second angle on it.

steps.prompt: What do you use the last light for?

options.text: Another take of the scene
options.detail: A second chance at the front angle. The film ends without its wide shot.
options.risks: a second take with faults of its own

options.text: The wide shot of the lighthouse
options.detail: The ending you planned. If take four has a fault, the side angle covers it.

choices.label: Move flat this spring

shown.name: Find out first
shown.because: Because you said news will come in time.

moves.name: Wait for it
moves.because: Because you said news will come in time.
moves.is: Holding off while the news arrives.
moves.costs: Whatever the wait costs in the meantime.
moves.breaks: When the risk grows faster than the news comes.
moves.like: hearing back from the second offer before answering the first

shown.name: Soften the step
shown.because: Because you said undoing it would cost something.

moves.name: Make it undoable
moves.because: Because you said undoing it would cost something.
moves.asks: Is there a version with an easier way back?
moves.is: A version of the step that is easier to reverse.
moves.costs: Whatever the way back costs: a fee, a trial’s limits, a longer route.
moves.breaks: When the way back costs nearly as much as the step.

shown.name: Keep it open
shown.because: Because you said waiting lets the chance go.

moves.name: Hold it open
moves.because: Because you said waiting lets the chance go.
moves.is: Paying to keep the chance while waiting.
moves.costs: What holding costs each week, needed or not.
moves.breaks: When nothing will be learned while it’s held.
moves.like: a deposit that keeps a place

moves.name: Ask for more time
moves.because: Because you said waiting lets the chance go.
moves.asks: Does someone else set the deadline?
moves.is: Asking whoever set the clock to move it.
moves.costs: Some goodwill, and sometimes the offer.
moves.breaks: When asking costs the offer itself.
moves.like: a week more before answering an offer

moves.name: Hand it over
moves.because: Because you said waiting lets the chance go.
moves.asks: Could someone else keep it going for now?
moves.is: Letting someone else hold it for a while.
moves.costs: What they do with it while it’s theirs.
moves.breaks: When they change what they hold.
moves.like: a friend subletting the flat for a year

moves.name: Keep it by using
moves.because: Because you said waiting lets the chance go.
moves.asks: Is using it what keeps it alive?
moves.is: Using a little of it, so it doesn’t fade.
moves.costs: Whatever the use takes from something else.
moves.breaks: When a little use isn’t enough to keep it.
moves.like: playing an instrument once a week so the skill stays

moves.name: Make another option
moves.asks: Is there a way through nobody has named yet?
moves.is: Looking for a way that isn’t on the list.
moves.costs: The time spent looking, while the others wait.
moves.breaks: When looking costs the chance there is.
moves.like: asking who else could use it

moves.name: Commit
moves.is: Taking the step now, on what is known.
moves.costs: Anything waiting would have taught, and any way back.
moves.breaks: When the answer was already on its way.

moves.name: Rule it out
moves.is: Deciding against it for good, and letting the question go.
moves.costs: Whatever the step would have brought.
moves.breaks: When the chance won’t come again, and there’s no other like it.
moves.like: telling the buyer no, and meaning it

moves.name: Set a tripwire
moves.because: Because you said waiting lets the chance go.
moves.asks: What would need to happen, and by when?
moves.is: Deciding now what would mean acting, or stopping, later.
moves.costs: A rule that may fire at the wrong moment.
moves.breaks: When it watches the wrong signal.
moves.like: a rule that if it isn’t paying by March, it stops

choices.note: Ask the landlord about a break clause.

options.text: Keep her, whatever happens
options.detail: She stays in the family, and so do the fees.

move.costs: fees for as long as you keep her
move.risks: a boat that never leaves her mooring

ask.label: Ask at the sailing club first
ask.answer: The club would take her for the season and teach beginners on her. No fees for you. She’d be theirs until October, so no sale before then, and beginners are hard on boats.

adds.text: Lend her to the club for the season
adds.detail: No fees, no sale until October, and beginners at the helm.

move.costs: a season of wear on her
move.risks: losing the buyer

cases.sell: The buyer sails her away on Saturday and promises a photo from the water. Your lessons start in a club dinghy. If you love it, there will be other boats, though not this one.
cases.summer: You pay the mooring and spend Saturdays sanding. By autumn you’ll know about sailing. Whether the buyer will still be interested, the story doesn’t say.
cases.always: You paint her name fresh on the stern. Whether you’ll sail her, the summer will tell. She’s yours either way.
cases.club: The club takes her for the season, and beginners learn on her, you among them. By October you’ll know about sailing, and she’ll have the scrapes to show for it.

ending.others: Some sell on Friday: a fair price is certain, and there are other boats to learn in. Some pay to keep the question open until the lessons answer it. Some keep her whatever happens.

shown.title: The new loaf
shown.hook: Eleven years of the same six breads. Now, maybe, a seventh.
shown.setup: Your bakery has sold the same six breads for eleven years, and your regulars like it that way. One night you worked out a seventh: dark rye with figs and fennel. You love it. You have no idea whether anyone else will.
shown.uncertain: Whether anyone but you will want the new bread.

steps.prompt: What do you do with it first?

options.text: Put twelve on the shelf on Saturday
options.detail: Costs a batch. If they don’t sell, you stop.

move.risks: loaves coming home unsold

options.text: Hand out tasting slices all week
options.detail: Costs a week and half a batch. You hear what people say.

move.costs: a week and half a batch
move.risks: kind words that never become sales

options.text: Give a loaf each to three regulars
options.detail: Costs three loaves. You hear from people who know your bread.

move.risks: three opinions standing in for everyone

cases.shelf: By closing time on Saturday, seven of the twelve have gone. A man in a green coat asks whether it will be there next week. Five come home with you.
cases.taste: All week the slices disappear. Most people say it’s lovely, a few say “interesting”, and one asks what fennel is. Nobody asks to buy a loaf.
cases.regulars: Two of them love it. Mrs Okafor says the fennel is far too strong, and that she’d buy it anyway.

options.text: Bake it every Saturday

move.risks: Saturdays of loaves coming home

options.text: Change the recipe, then try again

move.risks: losing what the first version had

options.text: Keep it as your own bread, not the shop’s

move.risks: never finding out

cases.weekly: It goes up on the board as the seventh bread. Over the winter you’ll find out what eleven years of regulars make of it.
cases.change: You take out half the fennel and try again in a fortnight. The rye stays dark.
cases.own: You bake it on Sundays, for the house. The six breads carry on as they were.

ending.others: Some put it straight on the shelf: a batch is cheap to lose, and only a sale shows who would buy it. Some ask first, because a shelf can’t tell you why a loaf didn’t sell.

shown.title: The last of the light
shown.hook: The best take of the day, and no way to see it until Thursday.
shown.setup: You’re directing a small film, shot on 16mm film. On the last evening at the lighthouse, take four of the farewell scene felt right: she held the pause before her last line. There’s light for one more set-up. Film can’t be seen until a lab develops it, and this evening’s reels come back on Thursday, after the crew has left the island.
shown.uncertain: Whether take four is as good on film as it felt on set.

steps.prompt: What do you use the last light for?

options.text: Another take of the scene
options.detail: A second chance if take four has a fault. The film ends without its wide shot.

move.risks: a second take with faults of its own

options.text: The wide shot of the lighthouse
options.detail: The ending you planned. Take four is your only good take.

move.risks: a fault in take four, with no other take

ask.label: Ask the camera operator about take four
ask.answer: She watched it through the lens. “The frame was right, and it looked sharp to me. On film, you only know on Thursday.”

cases.again: Thursday, at the lab. Take four is soft for two seconds, right on her last line. Take five is sharp throughout, and she rushes the pause. The film will end on her face, not the lighthouse.
cases.wide: Thursday, at the lab. Take four is soft for two seconds, right on her last line. An editor can cut away for those seconds, and lose her face as she says it. The wide shot is beautiful.

ending.others: Some shoot the scene again: the film can’t be checked, so a second take is the only cover. Some take the wide shot: take four felt right, and the ending matters too.

facts.fact: Film has to be developed before anyone can see what it caught. In the film era, each day’s footage went to a lab overnight and was watched later as “dailies”.

sources.name: Roland Denning, “The golden age of film laboratories”, RedShark News (2023)

facts.fact: On a film camera only the operator looks through the lens; the focus puller works from marks and judgement, and a soft shot can’t be made sharp afterwards.

real.invented: The film, the island, the takes and the lab’s Thursday are invented. Digital footage can be checked at once; this story is shot on film.

shown.title: The last packet
shown.hook: Ten rows, and a packet of beans nobody grows any more.
shown.setup: At the village seed swap, an old man presses a packet of climbing beans into your hand: a local kind nobody sells any more. Seeds this old don’t keep. Each year fewer will sprout, and in a few years none will. Your plot has ten rows, and your household eats from it all summer.
shown.uncertain: How many of the old seeds are still alive.

steps.prompt: How do you plant your ten rows this spring?

items.detail: Nobody knows how many will come up.

move.risks: a kind that stops sprouting
too few plants to save seed
rows standing half empty

cases.none: You keep the packet in a drawer, and the plot gives you its usual summer. Next spring, fewer of the beans will sprout; the spring after, fewer still.
cases.few: About one seed in three comes up. By September a handful of plants hang heavy with pods: just enough fresh seed to try again next year. The rest of the plot does what it always does.
cases.many: About one seed in three comes up, so those rows stand half empty and you buy vegetables in August. By September there is fresh seed to give away at next year’s swap.

ending.others: Some plant none: the household eats from those rows. Some give it a row or two, enough to save fresh seed. Some give it half the plot, because a kind that’s lost is lost for good.

facts.fact: Bean seed keeps for two to four years on average, longest when it is stored cool and dry.

sources.name: Johnny’s Selected Seeds, “Seed viability and seed storage guidelines”

real.invented: The packet, its age and “one seed in three” are invented.

shown.title: The old oak
shown.hook: Two hundred years old, and leaning over the school path.
shown.setup: The oak on the village green is about two hundred years old. It leans over the path to the school, and in March a big branch came down in the night. There is fungus at its base. The parish has left the decision to you, and the autumn storms are five weeks away.
shown.uncertain: Whether a hollowing, leaning oak will stand through the storms.

steps.prompt: Before you decide, you can find things out. Each takes time, and the work itself will need the last week.

facts.label: Ask the tree surgeon to climb it
facts.text: The crown is full of leaf. She says cutting it back would ease the strain, and that big cuts on an old oak can let rot in.

facts.label: Find old photographs of the green
facts.text: In a photograph from 1952 the oak leans exactly as far as it does today. There is no fungus in the photograph.

facts.label: Have the trunk scanned
facts.text: About a third of the trunk is hollow. Hollow oaks often stand for decades; some don’t.

move.risks: acting on a lean and some fungus alone
facts that still don’t settle it

options.text: Fell it
options.detail: No more risk from it, and no more oak.

move.risks: felling a tree that would have stood for decades

options.text: Take a third of the weight off the crown
options.detail: It stays, smaller. Less likely to fall; the cuts are for good.

move.costs: a third of the crown, for good
move.risks: rot in the cuts, or a fall anyway

options.text: Leave it, and fence off the path
options.detail: The oak stays as it is. The children walk round by the road.

move.costs: a longer walk to school while it stands
move.risks: the oak coming down inside the fence

cases.fell: The oak comes down in a day. The stump is wider than a kitchen table, and a boy from the school counts 214 rings. The path is open again by Friday.
cases.crown: The tree surgeon spends two days in the crown. From the pub the oak looks thinner, and still very much itself. The path stays open, and the storms will test it.
cases.fence: A fence goes up around the oak, and the school sends a letter about the longer walk. The oak meets the storms as it is.

ending.others: Some fell it at once. Some spend three weeks on the scan, because a felled oak can’t be put back. Some fence it off and let the children walk round.

facts.fact: A hollowing trunk is a natural process in old trees, and not necessarily a sign of an ailing one.

real.invented: The oak, the green, what each check finds and the five weeks are invented.
